analysis.one_liner: Requires mortgage brokers to put borrowers first and lenders to verify borrowers can repay.
analysis.headline: The Senate referred the bill to its Banking Committee the day it was introduced — May 3, 2007 — and it never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made mortgage brokers legally owe their loyalty to the borrower rather than the lender, and required every lender to verify with documents — tax returns, pay stubs, bank records — that a borrower could actually afford the loan, tested at the highest payment an adjustable rate could reach in its first seven years. It banned steering borrowers into loans that paid the broker more, made lenders responsible for broker misconduct on high-rate loans, and barred lenders from pressuring appraisers toward a target value. The Senate sent it to its Banking Committee the day it was introduced, and it never came up again.
analysis.who_benefits: People buying homes or refinancing — especially first-time buyers and borrowers with weaker credit, who were most often sold high-rate, no-documentation loans — would get a broker legally on their side, a verified ability to repay, honest appraisals, and a copy of the appraisal report. Borrowers in high-rate loans would get escrow accounts so taxes and insurance actually got paid.

how_it_helps.text: Makes mortgage brokers fiduciaries, legally bound to put the borrower's interest first and subject to all federal and state fiduciary requirements.

Requires lenders to verify a borrower's documented income and ability to pay principal, interest, taxes, and insurance before making a loan; the borrower's own statement is not enough, and adjustable-rate loans must be tested at the maximum possible payment for the first seven years.
Prohibits steering borrowers toward rates, charges, or prepayment terms that are not reasonably advantageous to them, and bars mischaracterizing a borrower's credit history or available loans.
Bars lenders from pressuring appraisers toward a targeted value and requires giving every applicant a copy of the appraisal report, whether the loan is approved or denied.
Makes lenders liable for a broker's acts and misrepresentations on high-cost rate-spread loans, and requires escrow accounts for taxes and insurance on those loans.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage brokers and lenders would bear compliance costs, lose no-documentation and steering-driven fee income, and face liability for broker conduct and appraisal pressure. Appraisers would have to carry a qualifying bond worth at least 1% of the homes they appraised the prior year. Some borrowers with strong finances but hard-to-document income would lose access to no-doc loans.

drawbacks.text: Requiring tax returns, payroll receipts, and bank records would end no-documentation lending, which some creditworthy borrowers — notably the self-employed with irregular but strong income — relied on to get mortgages.

Testing adjustable-rate loans at the maximum possible payment over the first seven years is a deliberately conservative standard that would disqualify some borrowers who could comfortably afford the payments they would actually owe.

The qualifying bond for appraisers — at least 1% of the total value of all homes they appraised the prior year — is a heavy fixed cost that would likely push smaller appraisers out of the business and concentrate the field.

Mandating escrow on high-rate loans raises the required monthly outlay for exactly the stretched borrowers most likely to hold them, even though it protects them from falling behind on taxes and insurance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core requirement — document that a borrower can afford the loan — targets the practice behind waves of unaffordable mortgages, and Congress enacted a similar ability-to-repay standard nationally in 2010 after the housing crash, which suggests the costs were manageable. The real costs fall on the industry's compliance budgets and on a narrower group of borrowers who used loosely documented credit, and the appraiser bond requirement is the crudest feature. On balance the protections outweigh the drawbacks; the bill's death left borrowers without these protections through the peak of the housing bubble.

outcome.mechanism: It never got a hearing or a vote — the Senate sent it to the Banking Committee the day it was introduced, and it sat there until that Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Charles Schumer introduced the Borrower's Protection Act of 2007 in the Senate on May 3, 2007, joined by Sens. Sherrod Brown and Bob Casey.
Six senators cosponsored the bill — five Democrats and one Independent; no Republican signed on.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the same day it was introduced.
No hearing, markup, vote, or report ever followed; the bill's last recorded action is the May 3, 2007 referral, and it died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage brokers and lenders came out ahead: they kept operating without fiduciary duties, mandatory income documentation, liability for broker and appraisal misconduct, or escrow requirements until after the housing crash, while borrowers got no federal protection in the meantime.

for.name: Sen. Charles E. Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Borrower's Protection Act of 2007 on May 3, 2007.

for.name: Six Senate cosponsors (five Democrats, one Independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the introduced text names Sens. Sherrod Brown and Bob Casey among its original supporters.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 3, 2007 and took no further action on it — no hearing, markup, or report appears in the record before the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, controlled the panel's agenda and never brought the bill up for consideration; the record shows no committee action after the referral.

sides.party_line_note: Every supporter on record was a Democrat or Independent — Schumer, five Democratic cosponsors, and one Independent — with no Republican signing on, and since the bill never reached a floor vote, a chamber-wide split was never tested.

industries.note: The bill made brokers fiduciaries of borrowers, banned steering and no-documentation lending, and imposed liability for misrepresentations — directly threatening fee income built on arranging loans borrowers could not sustain.
Lenders taking high-rate loans would become liable for broker misconduct and have to escrow taxes and insurance; the rules targeted the subprime segment where defaults and foreclosures concentrated.

The bill barred lenders from pressuring appraisers toward a target value, but required a qualifying bond of at least 1% of the prior year's appraised home values — a cost falling hardest on smaller firms.

industries.industry: Investors and banks buying packaged mortgages
industries.note: Verification requirements would have cut the volume of loosely underwritten loans available to buy and repackage, but reduced default losses on the loans that were made.
